title: Queue-pressure simulator and fairness probebook
content:
Purpose:
This note captures the design, runs, and preliminary analysis for a simulator-driven stress test that emulates queue-pressure conditions at the request-routing layer. Goal is to compare fairness strategies under adversarial and long-tail input shapes and to surface kernel-level hotspots that amplify tail latency during sustained pressure.

Background / motivation:
- Many previous experiments focused on batch formation heuristics in production traces. Those were indispensable, but they under-sample rare sustained pressure patterns (5–30s windows) that cause persistent p99 spikes and recovery hysteresis.
- We built a lightweight, parameterized queue-pressure simulator to generate repeatable, tunable stress windows (burst amplitude, sustained pressure duration, fraction of long-context requests, urgency skew). This allows controlled comparisons across fairness policies without noisy upstream traffic variability.

High-level hypotheses:
1) Under sustained queue pressure, "age-boost" policies maintain lower p99 latency for long-lived requests vs strict size-based coalescing but cost throughput slightly.
2) Proportional-share fairness (weighting by service-class) limits starvation but can increase average latency under high ctx-length variance.
3) Kernel overheads (small-kernel launches, CPU memcpy-to-GPU) become dominant contributor to p99 during high batch churn — not just batch size.

Simulator design (short):
- Request model: poisson base arrival + configurable burst injection. Each request has: token_count (short: 16–128, medium: 256–1024, long: 2048+), urgency (0..1), and a simple priority tag (service, background).
- Pressure window: parameters {burst_rps, sustained_seconds, decay_tau}. We sweep burst_rps from 2x baseline to 10x.
- Outcome metrics emitted per run: throughput (req/s), tokens/s, p50/p95/p99/p999 latencies, batch size distribution, preemption events, queue depth over time, fairness index (Jain's index over per-class latency), and kernel-level counters (CUDA launch count, memcpy ms, CPU scheduling stalls).
- Implementation: simulator integrates with local dev runtime harness so we can toggle real serving runtime vs mocked execution (fast-mode). Tracing uses the runtime's trace id and logs to perf-collector.

Policies compared:
- size-first: flush when batch reaches token-cap or timeout (baseline)
- age-boost: requests accrue urgency with queue time; urgency can upweight selection into batches
- proportional-share: per-service weight that enforces ratios at formation time
- capped-antique: prioritizes oldest requests but enforces a cap to prevent huge latency regressions for small requests

Runbook (how to reproduce locally):
1) checkout serving-runtime branch: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime branch queue-press-sim
2) run: ./dev/harness --simulator --policy=age-boost --burst=600 --sustain=20 --long_frac=0.1 --out=./out/ageboost-run1
3) collect traces: ./tools/collect-trace.sh ./out/ageboost-run1
4) upload with: python tools/upload_perf.py ./out/ageboost-run1 --dst perf-dash/probebook
Note: these flags map to the simulator spec in tools/simulator/README.md (see linked Confluence).

Key experimental settings used (summary table in text):
- Baseline arrival: 200 rps steady
- Burst amplitude: 600 rps (3x), 1200 rps (6x), 2000 rps (10x)
- Sustain durations: 8s, 20s, 60s
- Long request fraction: 0.02, 0.10, 0.25
- Token-cap per GPU batch: 48k tokens
- Flush timeout sweep: 5ms, 12ms, 25ms, 50ms

Representative run notes (selected interesting runs):
Run A (age-boost, burst=3x, sustain=20s, long_frac=0.10):
- p50: 7ms, p95: 28ms, p99: 84ms, p999: 230ms
- Average batch size: 18 requests (900 tokens avg)
- Fairness index: 0.86 (improved versus size-first 0.71)
- Kernel profile: memcpy host->device spikes correlate with p99 spikes (avg memcpy per batch increased by 3.4x during window). CUDA launch count increased 1.6x relative to steady-state (more small batches).
- Observation: age-boost prevented starvation of long requests; tail still high due to increased batch churn and memcpy overhead, not queueing alone.

Run B (proportional-share, burst=6x, sustain=20s, long_frac=0.25):
- p50: 9ms, p95: 48ms, p99: 220ms, p999: 880ms (very bad)
- Average batch size: 10 requests (1800 tokens avg) but high variance
- Fairness index: 0.93 (per-class latencies balanced)
- Kernel profile: kernel busy time high but dominated by long-context compute; small-batch launch overheads plus repeated preempt/resume created jitter.
- Observation: although per-class fairness metrics look good, aggregated p99 exploded because long requests serialize GPU compute and prevent batching efficiency; proportional-share allowed too many long requests to start early, reducing coalescing for short ones.

Run C (size-first with aggressive timeout = 5ms, burst=3x, sustain=8s):
- p50: 6ms, p95: 33ms, p99: 190ms
- Average batch size: 24 requests but many small batches during spike
- Kernel hotspots: CPU scheduling stalls increase during bursts — threads blocked waiting on IO for small copies.
- Observation: aggressive timeout reduces average latency but increases kernel launch overhead; tail suffers.

Profiling notes (how we gathered kernel-level data):
- We instrumented these layers: request-router (timestamps), batch-assembler (batch formation events), host->device memcpy timings (via CUPTI/metric API), kernel start/finish times (CUDA events), CPU thread scheduling latencies (schedtrace), and runtime internal queue lock hold times.
- The majority of observed p99 increases during pressure windows traced to three correlated phenomena: more frequent host->device memcpy calls due to smaller batches; higher kernel launch rate; increased contention for batch-assembly locks causing latency spikelets that cascade into p99.

Diagnostics and root-cause pointers:
- Memory copy inefficiency: when batches are smaller, the amortized memcpy per token is higher (higher driver overhead). We see this as longer memcpy_ms per batch even for identical token counts split across more batches.
- Kernel launch overhead: small batches cause more kernels to be launched overall; driver overhead and CUDA stream scheduling amplifies tail.
- Lock contention: batch-assembler holds a global lock briefly to splice request descriptors into a batch. Under pressure this critical section becomes a bottleneck; threads waiting for the lock show up as CPU scheduling stalls.

Quick mitigations tested in-situ:
- coalescing window slack: increase the flush timeout slightly during detected pressure windows (auto-scale timeout) — reduced p99 by ~25% in age-boost runs at cost of small increase to avg latency.
- batch-assembly lock sharding: split assembly locks by hash of request id to reduce contention (prototype): reduced CPU stall time by ~40% and p99 by ~15% in several runs.
- memcpy aggregation: use contiguous pinned staging buffer to aggregate small copies in fast-mode path — improved memcpy_ms by ~30% for small batches in the lab harness.

Open questions / follow-ups:
1) Can we implement an adaptive heuristic that trades off short-request latency vs amortized memcpy cost when long-request fraction spikes? Preliminary idea: detect long_request_fraction over sliding window and temporarily bias batch formation toward size (increase token limit) to keep memcpy amortization good.
2) How do preemption and kernel-level multi-tenant isolation interact with these policies on Dedicated hardware (multi-process GPU)? Need to run on a dedicated GPU machine with actual multi-tenant interference to validate lab improvements.
3) Is the fairness index (Jain) the right single-number summary? It hides the fact that proportional-share looked great on fairness but terrible for p999. Consider reporting a fairness-latency curve (latency per quantile per class).

Action items (next sprint):
- Implement lock sharding in batch-assembler (Diego) — target: prototype by 2025-03-07.
- Add adaptive timeout trigger (Sana) to the age-boost policy: heuristic based on sustained queue depth and observed memcpy_ms.
- Run Dedicated-machine validation (Markus) with mixed tenant load — schedule for 2025-03-10 test window.
- Add p999 telemetry per-class to perf dashboard and a 'pressure window' alarm for production to trigger simulations.

Appendix: useful commands/logs collected during experiments:
- dev harness cmd: ./dev/harness --simulator --policy=%POLICY% --burst=600 --sustain=20 --long_frac=0.1 --trace-collect
- perf trace collector: ./tools/collect-trace.sh ./out/%RUN%
- quick profile summary: scripts/quick_profile.sh ./out/%RUN% > ./out/%RUN%_summary.txt
- dashboard links: perf-dash/probebook (internal), traces/rt/2025-02-14/queue-sim-A
Notes to self (informal):
- The simulator is intentionally aggressive on long_frac to expose pathological cases. Real traffic rarely hits 25% long requests but when it does (e.g., document-summarize bursts) we saw dramatic impact.
- Keep experiment IDs in filenames; makes trace correlation much easier.
- When sharing with SRE/infra, include the kernel flame graphs; those made it obvious that driver calls were the hidden culprit.

End of probebook.

(If anything here looks like a duplicate of recent run notes, apologies — this is the canonical writeup consolidating lab runs A/B/C and action items.)
